extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for USPTO examiners on how to formulate subject-matter-eligibility rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and how to evaluate applicant responses using the two-part Alice/Mayo framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the judicial exception as recited in the claim (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the judicial exception by referring to what is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recites the judicial exception. Where the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the exception, the rejection must explain what subject matter those limitations describe and why that described subject matter is a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why the identified limitation corresponds to a court-identified abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner determines the claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as it is recited in the claim and explain why it corresponds to a concept that the courts have identified as an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing to an appropriate court decision that supports the identification is a best practice. Examiners should be familiar with any cited decision and ensure the rejection is reasonably tied to the facts. Examiners should not go beyond those concepts similar to what courts have identified as abstract ideas. See the July 2015 Quick Reference Sheet concepts for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why limitations recite a law of nature or natural phenomenon (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner determines the claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon, the rejection should identify it as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete reasoning (e.g., the claimed correlation describes a consequence of natural processes or occurs in nature and exists apart from human action). Use sample explanations where appropriate to show the connection to natural processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why a claimed product is a product of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim recites a product of nature, identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart (e.g., 'X in its natural state') and explain whether there is a marked difference in structure, function, or other properties. If no marked difference is shown in the record, treat as a product of nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional claim elements beyond the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify any additional elements (specifically point to claim features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the identified judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly call out which claim limitations are 'additional elements' to set up the Step 2B analysis. This should be concrete rather than generic labeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the reason(s) that the additional elements taken individually, and also taken as a combination, do not result in the claim as a whole amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address the additional elements both individually and in combination. Provide a reasoned rationale for the conclusion and explain why the combination does not meaningfully limit the exception. Remember that a new combination may be eligible (Diehr), so the combination analysis is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain when additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding that particular claim limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities in the relevant field, explain why the courts have recognized, or those in the field would recognize, those limitations as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior art search is not necessary to resolve this inquiry. The evaluation turns on whether the use was well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by those in the field. If determined widely prevalent and conventional, provide a reasoned explanation supporting that conclusion and consider rebuttal evidence to clarify the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat evidence of mere knowledge or limited use as proof of conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere discussion in journals or limited use by a few scientists does not automatically make a technique routine or conventional in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on whether the activity was widely prevalent and previously engaged in by the relevant scientific community. The standard is whether it was well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why generic computer components performing generic functions do not add significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, explain why these functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the July 2015 Update's listing of computer functions courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically. Do not assume all computer functions are conventional. Consider whether generic components in combination perform non-generic functions (e.g., DDR) and thus may be significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why extrasolution activity or field-of-use limitations are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extrasolution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, final storing step) or merely link the exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete reasoning; examples include storing data after computing a mathematical relationship or limiting an abstract idea to a particular industry (Flook-style) — such limitations often do not add significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples only as illustrative, not as bases for rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO examples issued with the Interim Eligibility Guidance are illustrative analyses and should not be used as a basis for subject matter eligibility rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (including hypothetical fact patterns) do not carry the weight of court decisions. Applicants may cite examples in support, but examiners should not require applicants to model claims after the examples to attain eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make rejections sufficiently clear and specific to enable effective response
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office action must provide an explanation as to why each claim is unpatentable that is sufficiently clear and specific to provide applicant sufficient notice of the reasons for ineligibility and enable the applicant to effectively respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the identified judicial exception, the specific additional elements, and the examiner's reasons for why those elements do not amount to significantly more, with a reasoned rationale tied to facts of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection only when conclusion is readily apparent to an examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on his or her expertise in the art in the Step 2B inquiry that the additional elements do not amount to claiming significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not readily apparent, avoid making a § 101 rejection. Where appropriate, explain why the additional elements provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully consider all applicant arguments and evidence when evaluating responses
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating an applicant response, examiners must carefully consider all of applicant's arguments and evidence presented to rebut the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant properly challenges the examiner's findings and persuasively establishes eligibility, withdraw the rejection. If maintaining the rejection despite a proper challenge, provide a rebuttal in the next Office action and consider rebuttal evidence to clarify the record for appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a reasoned rebuttal when maintaining a rejection after applicant challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant challenges the identification of an abstract idea based on a court case and the challenge is not persuasive, provide an explanation why the abstract idea identified in the claim is similar to the concept in the cited case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original rejection did not identify a Supreme Court or Federal Circuit decision and applicant challenges the identification, the examiner should point to a case with a similar abstract idea and explain why the claim corresponds to that case. Citation to a supportive case is not a new ground unless the basic thrust of the rejection changes (see MPEP 1207.03(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reevaluate when applicant provides specific evidence that elements are not conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant disputes that something is well-known, routine, conventional with specific argument or evidence, the examiner should reevaluate whether it is readily apparent that the additional elements are conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fully reevaluate especially when such elements are not discussed in the specification as known generic functions/components/activities or not treated by courts as conventional. If maintaining rejection, consider providing rebuttal evidence to support the conclusion and clarify the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess 'specially programmed' or 'particular machine' claims on whether they add significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant amends a claim to add a generic computer or generic computer components and asserts special programming or a particular machine, examine whether the added elements provide significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely adding a generic computer, generic components, or a programmed computer does not automatically overcome an eligibility rejection (Alice). Analyze whether the added elements meaningfully limit the claim, improve another technology, improve computer functioning, or add unconventional steps confining the claim to a particular useful application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption is not a standalone test for eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant argues that the claim does not preempt all applications of an exception, explain that preemption is inherent in and resolved by the Alice/Mayo two-part framework and is not a separate test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of complete preemption does not demonstrate eligibility; the two-step analysis addresses preemption concerns (as explained by Federal Circuit cases such as OIP and Sequenom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider combinations of generic elements as potentially amounting to significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an element does not amount to significantly more on its own, it can still amount to significantly more when considered in combination with other elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic computer components that individually perform generic functions may in combination perform functions that are not generic and therefore amount to significantly more than an abstract idea (see DDR). Examiners should analyze whether combinations meaningfully limit the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use court decisions as the primary foundation for identifications and conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: When identifying abstract ideas or other judicial exceptions and explaining why additional elements are conventional or not, the examiner should rely primarily on court decisions and reasoned rationale tied to facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chart of court decisions is available on the USPTO website. Ensure any cited decision is directly relevant and not taken out of context; be prepared to explain similarity to the instant claim if applicant challenges the citation.
